She moved around the shack gathering what she needed. A thornwood box from beneath the bed, its lid warped from damp. Copper wire coiled around a bobbin. A jar of beetle hearts in vinegar. The curved bone needle, carved from the rib of a child who had asked too many questions. Her old robe was gone, burned; she wore waxed canvas trousers and a fisherman’s sweater that smelled of smoke and eel. It would have to do.

At the threshold she paused and looked back. The shack was small, ugly, honest. Mud had tracked across her floor. For five years she had not spoken the name Adric aloud. Now it filled her mouth like a stone.

Outside, the marsh waited, gray and whispering. A flat-bottomed boat bobbed at the end of her dock, half-full of rainwater. She stepped in, her boots squelching, and took up the pole.

The courier did not follow. He was asleep, or he had fainted, and she did not wake him.

She pushed off. The fog closed around her like a hand.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The festival gate had swallowed Mira whole: tie-dye and body glitter, bass thumps and the smell of fried dough and warm grass. She clutched the photograph in her pocket—the one of her mother on a porch with a guitar, sun in her hair, smiling like the world was a song she already knew the words to.

She found the small stage at the far end of the grounds, the one made of pallets and Christmas lights. A woman with silver braids and a patched velvet coat was tuning an acoustic guitar, her back to the crowd.

Mira’s throat tightened. The woman moved the same way: head tilted, fingers restless, like she was always about to leave even when she was standing still.

“Stella,” Mira said.

The woman didn’t turn. “Set starts in ten, hon. Autographs after.”

“It’s Mira.”

The guitar string snapped. Stella’s shoulders went rigid. Slowly, she set the instrument down and turned around.

She looked older, thinner, the laugh lines around her eyes deeper, but it was her. The same sharp cheekbones, the same freckle at the corner of her mouth that Mira saw in the mirror every morning.

“Oh,” Stella whispered. “Oh, *Mira.*”

“Don’t say it like that.” Mira crossed her arms. “Like I’m a ghost.”

“I just—” Stella glanced toward the sound tent, then back. “How did you—who drove you here?”

“Nobody. I took a bus. Three of them. And a guy in a chicken costume gave me a ride the last mile.”

“You’re fourteen.”

“Yeah, I am. I can also read a schedule and pack a backpack. Amazing, right?”

Stella reached out, then stopped. “You can’t be here. Your dad—”

“Doesn’t know.” Mira stepped closer. “He thinks I’m at Emily’s. He thinks a lot of things. Like that you’ll send a birthday card. That you’ll call.”

Stella’s face crumpled, but she rebuilt it fast, the way people do when they’ve had a lot of practice. “It’s complicated, baby.”

“Don’t call me baby.”

“I’m sorry. I’m sorry, I just—”

“Why?” The word came out louder than Mira meant. A few festival-goers looked over. Mira didn’t care. “Why did you leave? Was it me? Was I too much? Because Dad said it wasn’t, but Dad also said you were ‘finding yourself,’ which sounds like something you tell a toddler when their dog runs away.”

Stella picked up the broken guitar string, wound it around her finger. “You were never too much. You were the best thing I ever did.”

“Then why weren’t you there?”

“Because I was scared.”

“Of what? Me?”

“Of *this.*” Stella gestured at the space between them. “Of looking at you and knowing I’d broken something I couldn’t fix.”

Mira laughed, short and harsh. “So you just… didn’t look? For three years?”

“I looked. I looked at your photos every day.”

“Photos aren’t people.”

“I know.” Stella’s voice cracked. “I know that, Mira. I’m not saying I was right. I’m saying I was a coward.”

Mira felt the familiar burn behind her eyes, the one she hated. She refused to cry here, in front of her mother and a guy selling hemp necklaces and the whole dusty festival.

“You missed everything,” she said. “I got my period and had to learn from a YouTube video. I made honor roll and Dad bought a cake that said *Congrats Mira* and we ate half of it on the couch. I got a solo in the winter concert and nobody recorded it because Dad’s phone died. I needed you.”

Stella closed her eyes. “I’m sorry.”

“That’s not enough.”

“I know.”

“You can’t just show up with sorry and a guitar and think—”

“I don’t.” Stella opened her eyes. They were wet, but her gaze was steady now. “I don’t think that. But I’m here. I’m right here.”

“For now.” Mira’s voice wobbled. “Until you pack up your van and disappear again.”

Stella was quiet for a long moment. The stage speakers hissed with feedback. Somewhere behind them, a drum circle started.

“I’m playing four more shows this summer,” Stella said. “Then I’m done with the road. I signed a lease last month. A real apartment. Two bedrooms.”

Mira stared at her. “You’re lying.”

“Come see the lease. It’s in my bag. It’s got a stain from a coffee cup and everything. Very official.”

“Why now?”

Stella finally stepped closer, close enough that Mira could smell her patchouli and sweat and the faint lemon of the tea she always drank. “Because I got tired of being scared. Because your sixteenth birthday is coming, then your graduation, then everything else, and I realized if I didn’t stop running, I’d miss all of it.”

“I don’t trust you,” Mira said. “I want you to know that.”

“That’s fair.”

“I’m still mad.”

“Also fair.”

Mira pulled the photograph from her pocket and held it out. “You left this. It fell behind the bookshelf when you packed.”

Stella took it carefully, like it might dissolve. “I thought I lost this years ago.”

“You did. I found it.”

Stella looked from the photo to Mira, and for the first time, she really seemed to see her. Not the idea of her. The actual girl: scraped sneakers, sunburned nose, chin raised like she was ready for a fight.

“You’re so much like me,” Stella said softly.

Mira’s jaw tightened. “I’m like Dad, too. He’s the one who taught me how to change a tire and how to make pancakes and how to show up.”

“Good,” Stella said. “Good. You should be like him.”

They stood there, the silence between them less like a wall now and more like a door someone had finally cracked open.

“I’m hungry,” Mira said.

Stella smiled, cautious. “There’s a falafel truck near the main stage. My treat.”

“I want two.”

“Two it is.”

“And you’re calling Dad before we eat. I’m not getting grounded because you’re scared of a phone.”

Stella nodded. “I’ll call him right now.”

“And you’re not allowed to cry while you do it. That’s my job.”

Stella laughed, surprised. “Deal.”

Mira didn’t take her mother’s hand as they started walking through the crowd. But she didn’t walk quite as far apart as she could have. The music swelled around them, loud and messy and alive, and for the first time in three years, Mira let herself believe that maybe—maybe—the song wasn’t over yet.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The shoe sat in front of Vassily Orlov like a loaded pistol. Eight decks, blue backs, the Casino Municipale crest gold-embossed in the corner. He tapped the edge with two manicured fingers. Not nervous. Just claiming territory.

Harrison Reeve didn’t reach for his whisky. He let it sweat on the baize beside his chips. Fifty thousand euros in plaques, cream and pink, stacked like compressed ash. He’d lost two hands already. That was fine. The money was Agency burn, and Orlov wasn’t here for the cash anyway. He was here because someone had told him an Englishman with a weakness for Punto Banco was asking questions in Marseille about shipping lanes.

“Noir,” Orlov said. He had a voice like gravel in oil.

The croupier slid a card face-down. Reeve didn’t look at it. He watched Orlov’s eyes instead. Small. Wet. The eyes of a man who’d moved from extortion to geopolitics and found the latter easier. He financed the network that had blown the consulate in Zagreb. Reeve had seen the photographs. The blackened masonry. The shrapnel patterns in the drywall.

Orlov peeled his card. The corner lifted a millimetre. His pupils didn’t change.

Reeve had been under for eight months. Long enough to forget the taste of decent tea. Long enough to let the alias settle into his marrow like rot. Tonight he wasn’t Harrison Reeve, failed commodity trader. Tonight he was just another desperate man trying to buy his luck back. Orlov needed to believe that.

The croupier dealt the second round. Reeve’s heart was doing something complicated against his ribs. Adrenaline, not fear. He’d learned the difference in Belfast.

“Carte,” Reeve said.

Another card. He didn’t touch it. House rules: only the dealer handled the shoe, but the ritual was the same. Baccarat was a stupid game, really. No skill. Just animal intuition and the mathematics of ruin. That made it perfect. You couldn’t bluff a man who understood probability, but you could bluff a man who thought he understood men.

Orlov smoked. A Gauloise, unfiltered, balanced on a crystal ashtray that had cost more than Reeve’s watch. Smoke curled between them like a curtain.

“You play tight,” Orlov said.

“I play to stay alive.”

Orlov smiled. It didn’t reach those wet eyes. “Then you should not have sat down.”

Reeve turned his cards. Seven. Orlov showed six. The croupier announced it in flat French. *Punto gagne.*

The chips scraped across the felt. Orlov didn’t flinch. But his jaw tightened. Not about the money. About the principle. Men like him hated losing control of the narrative, even for a second.

Reeve stacked the plaques. The room was too warm. The chandeliers too bright. Somewhere beyond the velvet rope, a woman laughed, and the sound was glass breaking. He needed Orlov to invite him upstairs. The private salon. That’s where the ledger was. That’s where the names of the cutouts lived, written in a Moleskine that Orlov carried like a rosary.

“Another?” Orlov asked.

“Until one of us breaks.”

Orlov lit a second cigarette from the first. “Or until one of us is already broken.”

He waved for the croupier to shuffle. New shoe. Fresh randomness. Reeve felt the weight of the ceramic pistol strapped to his ankle. He wouldn’t use it. Guns made noise, and noise made embassy press releases. But it was there. Solid. A reminder that he wasn’t what he appeared to be.

The cards fanned out. Orlov cut. The first card burned.

Reeve glanced at the mirrored pillar behind the bar. Just a flicker. His backup, a Polish cryptologic girl named Kasia, was supposed to be at the slots by now. She wasn’t. The reflection showed an empty stool and a half-finished martini melting in the heat.

Gone. Or taken.

Orlov followed his gaze. The smile returned, wider this time.

“Your luck,” Orlov said, sliding the shoe forward, “is not what it was.”

Reeve looked down at the untouched cards. His mouth tasted of copper. He was alone now. Exactly as planned, perhaps. Or exactly as Orlov had planned.

Either way, the next hand was for everything.

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
By February, Wren had stopped unpacking her suitcase. She lived out of it at ankle level, on the floors of hotel rooms that smelled of the same synthetic lavender from Manchester to Des Moines, and she could tell the day of the week by the coffee: burnt on the bus, watery at the VFW halls, surprisingly good at the megachurch in Cedar Rapids, where the pastor's wife took pity on her.

That morning it was a diner outside Concord, the kind with a counter that had survived four decades of candidates leaning on it. Dana, the communications director, found her by the pie case.

"You're on for the intro," Dana said. "Keep it under two minutes. The pancakes bit is testing well. And if anyone asks about school, you're 'taking a semester off,' not 'on leave indefinitely.'"

"I know."

"I know you know." Dana softened. "Your father's got the Boston thing tonight. He needs the family story to land here."

The family story. Wren took her mark behind the cash register, stage-left of the stool where her father would sit, and when the cameras came in with their soft explosion of light she did the fond laugh—the one she'd invented as a joke in October, miming a daughter's indulgence, and which was now in the briefing book under WREN: BEATS.

"Losing her mother nearly broke us," her father told the room, one hand wrapped around a mug he wouldn't drink from. "And I won't pretend I knew what I was doing. But I made pancakes. Every Sunday, no matter what. A man can get a lot said across a plate of pancakes."

Wren did the fond laugh. The room did its murmur. An old woman in a red hat reached for her wrist afterward and held it with the grip of someone who had buried people.

"Your mama would be so proud of you, honey."

"Thank you," Wren said. "She loved this part." She had no idea which part she meant. Her mother had hated politics with a completeness that Wren now understood as a form of love.

In the SUV between events, for eleven minutes, it was just the two of them and Marcus the body man up front, and her father let his face go slack the way he only did with the partition up, the candidate draining out of him like heat from an engine.

"You eating?" he asked.

"That's your line to the press."

"It's my line to you." He closed his eyes. "You did good back there."

"Dad."

"Hm."

"You never made pancakes."

Silence. The wipers went. Somewhere behind them the press bus labored through the slush.

"Rosa made pancakes," she said. "You ate them standing up, on the phone with Washington. Mom used to put a plate by your elbow like an offering."

"Rosa made them before. I'm talking about after. When it was just us."

"It was never just us. You were in D.C. three weeks a month."

He opened his eyes and looked at her, and for a moment she saw him deciding something—which father to be, here in the warm dark of the car with its tinted glass.

"Jack Calloway made pancakes," he said, almost gently. "Every Sunday. His daughter remembers it fondly." A pause. "I'm doing my best to keep up with him."

She should have been angry. Instead she felt the strange vertigo of watching him grieve correctly, publicly, in the grammar of a story, while the actual dead went unmentioned—her mother at the kitchen phone, saying Jack, your daughter needs you, saying it to a dial tone.

The SUV slowed. Marcus lowered the partition. "Ninety seconds, Senator. Wren, Dana says you're on for the intro."

Her father straightened his tie, and she watched him reassemble—the jaw first, then the eyes, then the man who made pancakes.

"Coming?" he asked, and it wasn't clear which of them he was asking.

She stepped out into the cold and the flashes, smiling like a daughter in a story.

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
I was the only person in the Hypo basement who thought the weather reports were lying.

Not lying in the usual way—every code lies, that is the point of a code—but lying *up*, building a fiction so tall and dull that nobody bothered to look underneath. For six weeks I had been copying the four-figure meteorological broadcasts out of the intercept logs, pasting them into a ledger in columns, and staring at them until the numbers swam. The JN-25 section got the glory and the windows and the extra ration of coffee. I got a card table under a pipe that dripped something brown at four in the morning, and a lieutenant commander named Bryce who believed anything not written in Japanese naval cursive was a distraction from the war.

“Kennedy,” he said, materializing behind me with the silent certainty of a man who had never been surprised by anything except his own promotion. “You’re still doing this?”

I did not look up. “Sir, the 0600 broadcast from Truk. The third group is a reciprocal of the 1800 broadcast from Kwajalein twelve days ago. Same cipher additive, but the raw underlying value is inverted by exactly one hundred.”

“That’s weather, Lieutenant. Weather is permitted to be boring.”

“It isn’t weather, sir.” I tapped the page with my pencil. The graphite made a soft *thock* against the ledger. “A typhoon east of the Marianas reports a pressure drop. Fine. But the wind-speed groups are never higher than twenty-two, and there hasn’t been a typhoon in the Western Pacific with winds below forty knots since June. The numbers are artificial. They’re placeholders.”

Bryce leaned over, close enough that I could smell the bay rum on his neck and the coffee on his breath. He was one of those men who treated proximity as an argument.

“You’re telling me the Japanese Navy,” he said, spacing the words like he was laying bricks, “has hidden an entire signal system inside *weather*?”

“No, sir. I’m telling you they’ve hidden traffic inside weather traffic. Low priority. Unclassified format. We don’t even bother sending it to Arlington.”

“Because it’s weather.”

“Because they made it look like weather.”

He straightened, and I knew before he spoke that I had lost. Not on evidence—evidence was something I still had in embarrassingly short supply—but on plausibility. In July of 1942, plausibility was a currency more valuable than oil. Pearl Harbor had happened because the imagination had failed. Now the imagination had swung hard the other way: every clerk with a hunch saw fleets behind every cloud. Bryce had seen too many hunches.

“Put it aside,” he said.

“Sir—”

“Forty-eight hours. On the main desk. Roche needs help with the latest additive recovery, and frankly, Kennedy, so do you.”

I watched him go, his shoes ticking on the concrete in a rhythm that sounded almost like code. *Put it aside.* As if suspicion were a necktie you could loosen after five o’clock.

“Don’t,” said a voice from the next table.

I turned. Vivian Corey sat under a green-shaded lamp with her hair pinned in a knot that looked as functional as a battleship rivet. She was a civilian, one of the Navy’s hired mathematicians, and she had the unnerving habit of answering questions people had not yet asked.

“Don’t what?” I said.

“Don’t put it aside. You have the look of a man about to obey an order he doesn’t believe in.”

I closed the ledger but kept my hand on it, possessive. “It’s weather, Viv. Commander Bryce says so. Who am I to argue with meteorology?”

“You’re the one who found the pattern.”

“I found *a* pattern. Patterns happen. Coincidences happen. The Japanese use a lot of fours and zeros because their operator’s finger gets tired.”

She laughed, not kindly. “You’ve been here since Tuesday. It’s Friday. Your collar looks like you’ve been sleeping in a map drawer, and you’ve got a pencil behind each ear because you ran out of places to put them. Men don’t do that for coincidences.”

I wanted to tell her about the map. I had not shown anyone the map. It lived in the bottom drawer, a Mercator projection of the Central Pacific on which I had plotted every suspect broadcast: Truk, Kwajalein, Jaluit, Ponape, Saipan. When you connected the artificial wind-speed groups with a straightedge and ignored the numbers the Japanese wanted you to read, the lines converged. Not on a fleet. On a schedule. Something was moving between the mandated islands at regular intervals, and the weather reports were counting the minutes.

But the map was still mostly empty space, and empty space frightened me more than contradiction. Empty space meant I had half a thought. Half a thought, in this building, was how you ended up transferred to a supply depot in Dutch Harbor.

“Bryce is right about one thing,” I said. “If I’m wrong, I’ve wasted six weeks. If I’m right, I still have to prove it before anyone will listen.”

Vivian picked up her own pencil and held it between two fingers like a cigarette. “Then prove it quietly. Don’t ask permission. Permission is how ideas go to die around here.”

“You’re suggesting insubordination?”

“I’m suggesting arithmetic. Keep your ledger. Work Roche’s desk for two days so Bryce sees a haircut and a clean shirt. Meanwhile, I’ll pull the August intercepts from the file room. Weather traffic, merchant call signs, anything in the clear. If your ghost is real, it will have left footprints in ordinary paper.”

I looked at her. The lamp made a bright island of her desk and left her eyes in shadow.

“You believe me?”

She tilted her head. “I believe the numbers. Numbers are patient. They don’t care whether you’re a lieutenant or a commander or the Emperor’s nephew. They only care if you’re paying attention.” She smiled. “And you, my dear Kennedy, are paying attention like a man who owes money to the alphabet.”

I opened the ledger again. The figures waited for me, neat and indifferent. Somewhere above us, in the real world, the sun was rising over the harbor, turning the water the color of gunmetal. Somewhere across the ocean, a radio operator in a tropical uniform was tapping out a string of four-digit groups that looked like barometric pressure and smelled like prelude.

I picked up my pencil.

“Forty-eight hours,” I said.

“Thirty-six,” Vivian corrected. “If whatever you’re hearing is moving on a schedule, we don’t have forty-eight.”

I did not ask her what she thought was moving. I was afraid she would say it first.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The Greyhound bus wheezed to a stop at the corner of Maple and Third, and Clara stepped onto the curb with one suitcase and twelve years of avoidance. Millbrook looked smaller than she remembered, as if the town had drawn in its shoulders against the October wind. The leaves were turning—burnt orange and rust red—and the air smelled of wood smoke and someone’s distant bonfire.

She had not planned to come back. Then her mother’s call came, thin and careful, and the magazine assigned her a feature on dying Main Streets, and suddenly the past was a place with a train schedule.

Clara adjusted the strap of her bag and started down the sidewalk. She had not made it past the pharmacy when she saw him.

He was propped against the bed of a battered blue pickup, arms crossed, laughing at something the man beside him had said. His hair was darker now, cut shorter, and there was a scar above his left eyebrow that she did not recognize. But the slope of his shoulders, the way he tilted his head when he listened, the easy grin that had once been hers alone—those were unchanged.

Tristan Hale.

Her feet stopped before her mind could catch up. A dog barked. A leaf spiraled down between them. Then he looked up.

For a second, something flickered across his face—surprise, maybe, or the ghost of old injury. He straightened slowly, never breaking eye contact.

“Clara.”

It was not a question.

“Tristan.” Her voice came out steadier than she felt. “Hi.”

The man beside him glanced from one to the other, mumbled something about a delivery, and vanished around the corner of the hardware store. Tristan did not move. He was wearing a flannel shirt with the sleeves rolled up, and his forearms were dusted with sawdust. A carpenter now, she remembered her mother saying. He built things. Fixed what was broken.

“You’re back,” he said.

“For a little while.”

“How long is a little while?”

“A week. Maybe two.”

He nodded, absorbing this. A muscle worked in his jaw. “You look good.”

“So do you.”

The compliment hung in the air, awkward and insufficient. She wanted to say more—wanted to explain that she had been eighteen and frightened, that the scholarship letter had arrived the same week his father died, that leaving without a note had been the cowardice of a child who did not know how to hold grief and hope in the same hand. But the words jammed in her throat, the way they always had.

Tristan pushed off the truck. Up close she could see the flecks of gold in his brown eyes, the small lines at their corners. He smelled of pine and fresh-cut wood.

“Coffee?” he asked.

She blinked. “What?”

“There’s a place two blocks down. New since you left. Decent muffins, terrible jazz.” He almost smiled. “Unless you’ve got somewhere to be.”

Her mother was waiting. The feature needed research. There were a hundred reasons to say no.

“Okay,” she said.

They walked in silence at first, the kind that scraped and pulled at old wounds. Millbrook had changed more than she thought: a yoga studio where the video store used to be, a wine bar where she and Tristan had once shared a milkshake on a dare. But the oaks were the same, and the library steps, and the bronze plaque commemorating the flood of ’98, which they had once climbed in the rain because he had wanted to kiss her somewhere historic.

“Why’d you come back?” he asked.

“Work. And my mom.”

“That all?”

She glanced at him. “What else would there be?”

He was quiet for a moment. Then: “I don’t know, Clara. You’re the one who left.”

The words were mild, but they landed hard. She wrapped her arms around herself.

“I know.”

“You could’ve said something. A note. A phone call. Hell, a text message would’ve been revolutionary back then, but you didn’t even leave that.”

“I was scared.”

“Of what? Me?”

“Of staying.”

He stopped walking. They stood in front of the coffee shop, its window fogged with warmth, and for a moment the twelve years between them seemed very thin, a curtain she could push aside if she only had the courage.

“You broke my heart,” he said quietly. “You know that, right?”

“I broke mine too.”

She hadn’t meant to say it. The honesty felt dangerous, a loose thread she could not stop pulling. Tristan studied her face as if searching for the girl she had been, the one who had kissed him behind the bleachers and sworn she would never leave.

“Did you ever think about coming back?” he asked.

“Every day for the first year. Then less. Then only when it rained, or when I heard a certain song, or when I met someone and realized he didn’t laugh the way you did.”

Tristan’s expression softened by degrees. He reached out, then hesitated, his hand hovering near hers before falling away.

“I built the porch on your mom’s house last spring,” he said. “She told me you were in Chicago. A journalist.”

“She mentioned you too.”

“What did she say?”

“That you never married.”

Something flashed in his eyes—surprise, then caution. “She say why?”

“No.”

He looked away, toward the street, where a child in a red coat was chasing leaves. “I told myself it was because no one here was worth the trouble. But that was only half true.”

Clara’s pulse thudded in her ears. “And the other half?”

He met her gaze. “The other half was still waiting for you to explain why you left.”

The coffee shop door opened, releasing a burst of warmth and the sound of laughter. Neither of them moved.

“I’m sorry,” Clara said. The words were small, inadequate, but she said them anyway. “I’m so sorry, Tristan. I thought I was chasing a life. I didn’t realize I was running from one.”

He was silent for a long moment. Then he reached for her hand, his fingers rough and warm and familiar, and she let him take it.

“One week,” he said. “Maybe two.”

“That’s all I have.”

He squeezed her hand gently. “Then we’d better stop wasting it.”

And for the first time since she had stepped off the bus, Clara felt the past loosen its grip—just a little, just enough to let her breathe.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
October 14th

The hydrangeas are wilting again. I told the florist at the hospital gift shop that white means resilience, not funerals, but he simply nodded with that vacant smile people reserve for grief. As if grief is a single, tidy emotion. I had to arrange them myself—three stems, angled precisely—because the nurses here have no sense of symmetry. None at all.

Nurse Simmons clicked in at 9:15, her crepe-soled shoes squeaking like mice. She thinks I don't notice the way she hovers by the vitals monitor, but I notice everything.

"His pressure's steady today, Mrs. Cole. That's good."

"Claire, please. We're practically family by now." I shut the diary—not that I hide it; secrets are for people who haven't learned that transparency is the ultimate disguise. "Did he move at all? Any flicker?"

"Nothing significant." She adjusted the IV bag, her fingers too rough on the tubing. "The doctor will round this afternoon. We'll discuss reducing the sedation then."

I smiled, the one that crinkles the corners of my eyes. David always said it made me look like a photograph from the 1950s. "Reducing it? So soon? He only just... settled."

"It's protocol. We need to assess neurological function."

"Of course. Protocol." I ran my thumb over David's knuckles. His hand is still elegant, even with the bruising from the drip. "He's always been such a deep sleeper. Haven't you, darling? Remember our honeymoon? I couldn't wake you for the continental breakfast. You said, 'Claire, let me drown in peace.'"

Nurse Simmons paused. "Mrs. Cole—Claire—you should take a walk. Get some air."

"I have excellent circulation, thank you."

When she left, the door clicked with hospital finality. I leaned close to his ear. The antiseptic smell can't mask his cologne, that stupid woody scent he wears because his secretary once said it smelled like authority.

"You couldn't even do this right," I whispered. My lips brushed his earlobe. "A nautical knot, David. You used a nautical knot. Who ties a bowline to die? You looked like a failed marionette. If you wanted to leave me, you should have used pills. Neater. Quieter. Considerate."

His chest rose and fell, obedient machine.

I opened the diary again.

Last Tuesday feels like a smudged watercolor. I came home at 6:30—the salmon was resting, the wine breathing—and there he was. Suspended. The chair overturned like a question mark. But here's the thing no one asks: the rope was too long. His toes were brushing the floorboards. Did he think I wouldn't check the garage? Did he think I'd let him embarrass us both with an amateur performance?

I cut him down. Of course I did. I cut him down and I breathed into his mouth—my breath, forcing life back where he tried to steal it—and then I called 911. I was very calm. I told them, "My husband has had an accident." Because suicide is so theatrical, isn't it? So demanding.

The memory tastes like copper. I remember shaking him, my hands on his shoulders.

"Look at me," I'd said. "Look at me, you coward. You don't get to quit. You don't get to vanish and leave me explaining your absence to the neighbors. We had a deal."

His eyes had rolled back, fluttering. For one second—one delicious second—I thought he'd heard me.

Now the doctors speak in hushed tones about "hypoxic injury" and "waiting." As if we're waiting for a train. I sit here and I hold his hand and I speak to him in the voice I use for dinner parties.

"Margaret called," I told him this morning. "She wants to visit. I said Wednesday, but only for fifteen minutes. She always did look at you too long at Christmas. I won't have her weeping on your shoulder while you're unconscious. It's undignified."

I adjusted his pillow. Too hard, perhaps. His head lolled.

"And the bank left a message. About the safety deposit box. The one I didn't know about." I smoothed his eyebrow. "You're going to wake up, David. You're going to wake up and tell me the combination, and then you're going to tell me her name. Again. Slowly. So I can write it down properly. Because if you think lying here like Sleeping Beauty absolves you—"

The monitor beeped, a sharp arrhythmia. I stopped. I smiled.

"Steady," I said, to him or to the machine, I'm not sure.

I think about the rope sometimes. The way it creaked. The way his throat looked, striped red. But mostly I think about the note they didn't find because I found it first, folded in his breast pocket like a love letter. Four words: *I can't breathe anymore.*

How melodramatic. How utterly unfair. I was the one who couldn't breathe, all those nights he came home smelling of her. I was the one suffocating in our perfect house, our perfect life.

Nurse Simmons is back in the corridor. I can hear her laughing with someone. They think I'm devoted. The devoted wife in her cashmere cardigan, writing her little book, waiting for her tragic husband to return.

They don't know I checked the knot twice before I called.

They don't know I made sure it was just tight enough.

Write. Breathe. Close the book.

Wake up, darling. We have so much left to say.

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
The third sheet had it too.

Reese sat back and pressed the heels of his hands into his eyes until he saw stars. The bulb over his desk threw a cone of yellow light onto the intercepts, and beyond it the Dungeon hummed along — tabulators clacking, a fan shoving hot air from one corner to the other, McGuire's radio murmuring dance music at two in the morning because nobody had the heart to tell him to shut it off.

*AF.* Again.

He'd logged it eleven times in six days. AF wanted water. AF was short on refrigeration tonnage. AF sat dead center in a strike plan wrapped around a date that kept half-translating itself into the first week of June. Half the groups were garble — static, a sleepy radioman copying on a mill up at Heeia — but every time the recovery boys peeled another layer off JN-25, AF got bigger. Hungrier.

And it wasn't Dutch Harbor, no matter what Washington said.

He carried the worksheets down the corridor, past the cots where off-duty men slept in their skivvies, and laid them in front of Lieutenant Commander Denton. Denton read with a cigarette parked in his teeth. Took him four minutes. Reese counted every one.

"AF." Denton tapped the page. "Could be anything. Garrison in the Marshalls. Could be the canal."

"With a water problem? Sir, the canal doesn't run dry."

"Midway does." A pause. Ash fell on the desk. "So does every rock in the Pacific." He slid the sheets back. "You're seeing shapes in noise. Happens. Go sleep it off."

"I've been sleeping it off since Tuesday. The pattern holds."

"It's an inkblot, Lieutenant. Stare long enough, you'll see whatever you walked in believing."

Reese gathered up the worksheets. His hands were steady, which surprised him, because the rest of him was shaking — coffee, fatigue, the old December anger that never really left the building. They'd all been wrong once. Wrong on a Sunday morning, wrong in a way that left the harbor burning for two days. Being wrong had a smell out here. Fuel oil and worse. So nobody in the Dungeon wanted to be wrong twice, and the safe play was to see nothing, call everything an inkblot, and let Washington do the thinking.

Washington. He'd read the last estimate himself — OP-20-G leaning toward the Aleutians, maybe a push at Fiji, anything but a place two letters wide on a chart.

He found Rochefort in the back office, feet up, wearing that damned velvet smoking jacket over his khakis like a man playing cards in somebody else's war. The commander read the worksheets twice. Said nothing for a long while. The fan ticked overhead.

"Denton thinks I'm chasing ghosts," Reese said.

"Denton's careful. Careful keeps you employed."

"It keeps you blind, too."

Rochefort's eyes came up. Pale, amused, tired to the bone. "You've got a designator and a feeling, son. Nimitz can't bet the last carriers in the Pacific on a feeling."

"Then let's stop feeling." Reese heard the idea as he said it — he'd been turning it over for days without knowing, and now it came out whole. "Make them tell us. Put Midway on the open circuit, plain language, no code: their water condenser's busted, they're down to a week's supply. If Tokyo's listening and AF is Midway, some analyst on their side passes it up the line. Two days. Three. We read our own answer in their traffic."

Silence. The tabulators clacked on down the hall.

Rochefort took his feet off the desk. He folded the worksheets once, neat, and tucked them inside his blouse like a love letter.

"Draft the message," he said. "And Reese — don't you dare be wrong."

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The black sedan crested the palace hill at midnight, rain lashing the windshield. Elara Vane did not look at the spires. Five years since she had been driven down this same road in the opposite direction, her robes stripped of sigils, the prince’s judgment ringing in her ears. Now the gates opened again, and guards in Kevlar with silver ward pins on their collars let the car pass without meeting her eyes.

She had not brought a staff. She wore no court colors—just a charcoal coat over a cable-knit sweater, jeans scuffed at the knees, and the iron ring on her right hand that exile had not taken because he did not know what it was. The ring was old, older than the monarchy, and it was already beginning to itch.

A palace aide met her in the marble atrium. “Mage Vane. Thank you for coming.”

“I came for the fee,” Elara said. “Not your thanks.”

The woman flinched. Beyond the vaulted lobby, emergency mages in sterile white hurried past with cases of crystallized aether. Above them, oil portraits watched with gilded disapproval, modern security cameras blinking beside the frames like tiny, judgmental eyes.

“His Royal Highness is in the Sunrise Suite,” the aide said. “He collapsed at noon. The court physicians believe it is a curse, but they cannot identify the—”

“I’ll see for myself.”

The aide hurried to keep pace as Elara climbed the grand staircase two at a time. The palace smelled the same—beeswax, old velvet, and the ozone tang of protective wards. At the third floor, a silver door stood guarded by two royal mages whose hands glowed faintly with ready defensive spells.

“She’s cleared,” the aide gasped.

The spells flickered out. The door opened.

The prince was not unconscious. That was the first surprise.

Prince Cassian sat propped against a mountain of pillows in the canopied bed, pale as parchment but awake, dark hair matted to his forehead. A heart monitor beeped beside him, its digital rhythm out of sync with the slow pulse of the curse-thread Elara saw coiled around his chest—a black vein of magic eating its way toward his heart. She could smell it now, beneath the antiseptic: wet stone and rotting flowers.

His eyes found hers. They were the same storm-gray she remembered.

“You came,” he said.

“Your chancellor offered a blank check.” She stepped to the bedside, ignoring the court physician who hovered nearby with a clipboard. “Also, he implied my apartment would be searched by the Crown Wardens if I refused. Flattery and threats—very on-brand.”

Cassian’s mouth twitched. “I told him not to threaten you.”

“And yet here I am, summoned by the man who once swore I would never set foot in his palace again.”

The physician cleared his throat. “Mage Vane, the curse—”

“I see it.” Elara pulled off her coat and tossed it over a chair. The iron ring was warming fast now, turning from gray to faint silver against her skin. “A soul-anchor. Somebody tied His Highness to a dying thing—a tree, an animal, perhaps another person. Every breath he takes pulls the anchor closer to death, and it pulls him with it. Sloppy, ancient work. The kind they used to bind rivals in the old wars.”

Cassian watched her, silent. The old arrogance was gone from his face, or maybe the curse had simply eaten it.

“Can you break it?” the physician asked.

“Yes.”

“Then please—”

“It will cost him something. It always does.” She looked directly at Cassian. “When I cut the anchor, the backlash will take a memory. One you value. That’s how the curse is built.”

Cassian closed his eyes. “Do it.”

“You don’t want to know which memory?”

“I trust you to choose.”

Elara laughed, sharp and short. “The man who exiled me for ‘reckless and self-serving magic’ now trusts me with his soul.”

“You were reckless,” Cassian said quietly. “You were never self-serving. I was angry, and I was wrong. I have spent five years knowing it, and three days wishing I had said so before I collapsed.” He drew a shallow breath. “Choose the memory, Elara. Choose the one that hurts most, if it buys me tomorrow.”

The heart monitor stuttered. The black thread pulsed.

Elara laid her hand over his heart. The iron ring flared white, burning cold against her knuckle. For a moment she felt the shape of the thing that bound him—a tree in a distant forest, its roots drinking poison, its leaves already brown. Then she reached in, found the knot, and pulled.

“You always did like grand gestures,” she said. “Hold still, Your Highness. This is going to humiliate us both.”

The light swallowed the room.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The rain in Westmarch falls like it’s personally offended by you. Cold, vertical, and somehow in your boots before it ever hits the ground. I know this because I’ve trudged through three counties of it, and the fourth—the one currently trying to drown the village of Hallow’s End—felt exactly the same.

“You’re scowling,” Bramble said.

“I’m concentrating.”

“You’re scowling at a puddle. I can hear it from up here.” He shook his entire body, sending a fan of muddy water across my already-drenched cloak. “Also, you smell like a dead trout that’s been to university.”

“And you smell like wet dog.”

“I *am* wet dog. It’s an honest profession. What’s your excuse?”

I didn’t answer. He was right, and we both knew it, and arguing with a talking hound in public never improved anyone’s reputation. Instead I squinted at the inn ahead, which had a sign reading THE SLEEPY HARVEST in letters so faded they looked like a threat. Villages called Hallow’s End and inns called The Sleepy Harvest never hired you for anything pleasant. They hired you because something had crawled out of a grave and started eating the heirs.

The door swung open before I reached the step.

A woman filled the frame, broad as a cider press and twice as red in the face. She held a rolling pin like a sword. Behind her, a dozen pale faces peered over tankards.

“You the hunter?” she demanded.

“Depends. You the one with the walking departed?”

“We don’t say corpse here,” she said stiffly. “We say departed.”

“Fine. You got departed strolling around after curfew?”

The rolling pin dipped an inch. “Two of ’em. Old Man Piers and the miller’s boy.”

I did some quick arithmetic. Two revenants, probably feral, likely a nest nearby. Standard rate was three silvers per head, plus hazard if they were fresh. “I charge six silver for the pair. Eight if they’ve killed anyone.”

A man in the back—someone important by the way his belly entered the room before the rest of him—stood up. “That’s robbery.”

“That’s inflation. Corpses are heavier than they look.”

Bramble sneezed, which was his version of a laugh. “She’s also half-vampire, so you’re getting a professional discount on the embarrassment.”

I kicked him. Not hard. He was still my dog.

The woman with the rolling pin narrowed her eyes at me. I was used to it. They always looked for the signs: the too-pale skin, the faint point to the canines, the way I didn’t breathe quite right. I’d been told my eyes caught lamplight like a cat’s—charming as a child, inconvenient when haggling.

“Half-vampire,” she repeated. “Does that mean you drink blood?”

“Only when it’s on the menu.”

“Is it?”

“Not yet.” I smiled, showing just enough fang to be honest but not enough to start a riot. “Look, I can stand in your rain and discuss my dietary habits, or I can go find Old Man Piers before he finishes digesting your chickens. Your choice.”

Bramble flopped onto the porch, resting his chin on his paws. “Tell her about the free consultation. People love free consultations.”

“Shut up.”

“The dog talks,” the woman said flatly.

“Unfortunately.”

“He’s also filthy.”

“That part’s optional.”

She studied us for a long moment—me in my stained leather, Bramble in his matted fur, both of us dripping on her threshold like something the river had coughed up. Then she stepped aside.

“Come in. Morris will show you where they rose. And you’ll take four silver.”

“Seven.”

“Five.”

“Six, and the dog gets a bowl of scraps.”

Bramble lifted his head. “I prefer the term *artisanal leftovers*.”

“Deal,” the woman said, “but if you bite anyone living, girl, I’ll personally introduce your skull to this rolling pin.”

“Fair enough.”

Inside, the hearth was warm and the ale smelled like bread and regret. I should have been relieved. Instead, my stomach twisted—not from hunger, though that was there too, a hollow little hum behind my teeth, but from the wrongness threading through the room. It was faint, a cold wire pulled tight beneath my ribs. The dead were close. Not in the inn, but near. And more than two.

I leaned down and whispered to Bramble. “We’ve got company.”

He stopped shaking and went very still, one ear cocked toward the dark beyond the windows. “How many?”

“I’m not sure. More than the brochure promised.”

“Wonderful. Remind me again why I left the crypt?”

“Because I carry the snacks.”

He sighed, a long rumble that ended in a whine. “Right. Let’s go earn our artisanal leftovers.”

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
Claire stepped through the swinging doors into the hotel's service corridor, her heels clicking against the anti-slip rubber flooring. The kitchen had emptied an hour ago after the rehearsal dinner cleanup, leaving only the industrial hum of refrigeration units and the faint, bleach-and-grease scent of a scrubbed-down line. She was here for one final check—the bride had insisted on hand-dried lavender garnish for the morning's welcome mimosas, and Claire trusted no one else to verify the storage conditions.

Her breath didn't mist yet. That changed when she reached the walk-in freezer at the corridor's end.

The heavy stainless-steel door stood ajar by three inches. That alone sent a needle of irritation up her spine. She'd coordinated events at the Meridian for six years; Chef Rodrigo ran a tight ship, but his night crew had a lazy habit of kicking the door shut without latching it properly. Energy waste. Food safety violations. Claire catalogued the sins as she reached for the handle, her fingers brushing the frosted metal.

She pulled.

The blast of cold hit her like a physical wall, stealing the air from her lungs. Negative eighteen, probably. Her silk blouse offered no protection. Inside, the overhead LEDs cast a clinical, blue-tinged glow across towering wire racks laden with cryo-vacced salmon, butter bricks wrapped in wax paper, and sheet pans of frozen petit fours for tomorrow's three-hundred-guest reception. Fog curled around her ankles, thick as dry ice, swirling as she stepped inside.

"Hello?" Her voice died against the insulated walls. She reached for the light switch out of habit, though it was already on. "Is someone in here?"

Then she saw the shoe.

It was a black patent leather Oxford, size eleven maybe, polished to a mirror shine that reflected the LED panels overhead. It pointed toward the dairy shelf at an awkward angle, as though the foot inside had twisted at the last moment. Claire's professional mind noted the incongruity—street shoes in the kitchen's sterile zone—before the rest of her caught up.

She moved around the endcap. The fog parted.

Ethan lay on his side between a crate of champagne grapes and a pallet of beef tenderloin. His tuxedo jacket was open, the cummerbund askew, the crisp white shirtfront still starched but now dusted with a fine layer of crystalline frost. His eyes were open. That was the worst part—they were open, pale blue irises filmed over, staring at nothing with an expression of mild surprise, as if death had arrived mid-sentence. His lips had gone the color of ripe plums. A delicate tracery of ice glittered along his hairline and in the stubble of his jaw. The gardenia boutonnière pinned to his lapel had wilted and then frozen, its white petals now brittle and translucent as glass.

Claire's clipboard slipped from her fingers. The metal edge struck the floor with a clang that should have been deafening but sounded muffled here, swallowed by cold and steel.

"Oh, God. Oh, no." She pressed her hand against her mouth. Her exhale plumed wildly. "Ethan?"

She knew better. She knew from the absolute stillness of his chest, from the rigidity of his fingers curled against the diamond-plate floor, from the way the frost had already settled into the weave of his jacket like a second skin. He'd been here for hours. But protocol—her frantic, desperate protocol—demanded she check.

She knelt. The cold burned her knees through her trousers. Her fingers trembled as she reached for his wrist. The skin was ice, hard and unyielding as wax. She found no pulse, only the stiff resistance of a body that had surrendered to the room's relentless chill. A thin gold watch on his wrist had stopped at 11:47.

"Claire?" A voice from the doorway.

She jerked backward, cracking her elbow against a shelf. Boxes of frozen butter tumbled. Jorge, the night engineering manager, stood silhouetted against the warm light of the corridor, his maintenance cart behind him. He wore his navy uniform and a confused frown.

"Why's this door open? You're gonna trip the—" He stopped. His gaze tracked from her face to the floor. His mouth opened, closed. "Jesus. Jesus Christ. Is that...?"

"It's Ethan," Claire heard herself say. Her voice sounded like it belonged to someone else, someone standing very far away in a warm room. "The best man. He's... Jorge, he's dead."

Jorge didn't move. His hand remained on the door handle. "You touched anything?"

"No. I mean—his wrist. I checked for a pulse." She tried to stand, but her legs were shaking. The cold had sunk into her bones, making her joints ache. "Call 911. Now."

Jorge finally stepped inside, letting the door hiss shut behind him. The latch engaged with a hollow, final click that made Claire's stomach turn. He didn't seem to notice. He was staring at the body, at the way Ethan's frozen limbs locked him in his final posture. "We need to get out before we freeze. Come on. Up."

But Claire wasn't looking at Ethan anymore. She was looking at his right hand. It wasn't empty.

Her knees had gone numb, but she leaned forward anyway, close enough to smell the iron-and-alcohol scent that lingered beneath the freezer's sterile air. Ethan's fist was clenched tight, the knuckles white and frozen in their grip. Protruding from between his rigid fingers was a scrap of heavy cream cardstock—the kind the hotel used for its premium stationery, the kind she'd approved for the welcome bags just that afternoon. Something was written on it, the ink already feathering slightly from the condensation that had frozen and refrozen.

"What is it?" Jorge asked, his voice dropping to a whisper. He reached for her shoulder. "Claire, don't touch it. The cops—"

"Don't," she read aloud. Her breath clouded over the word.

Jorge blinked. "Don't what?"

"That's what it says. Just... Don't."

Outside, in the corridor, the hotel's climate control sighed and cycled on, carrying with it the distant, muffled thump of bass from the hotel bar where the groom's party was still drinking whiskey and pretending that tomorrow would be perfect. Here, in the artificial winter, Claire Donovan felt the first true frost of the evening settle somewhere deep behind her ribs.

She looked at the door. She looked at the scrap of paper. And she realized, with the terrible clarity that would haunt her for the next forty-eight hours, that someone had locked Ethan inside with a warning—and left him to turn to ice among the wedding canapés.

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
Cellar Hole

The dog came with the house. That was never in the listing — 4 BR FARMHOUSE, 11 ACRES, SEBAGO, SOLD AS-IS — but when Dan Mercer coasted the U-Haul up the driveway on the first of October, the dog was on the porch waiting, a yellow mutt with a gray muzzle and a collar worn smooth as an old belt. It watched them carry in the boxes. It did not bark.

"That's Banjo," said the woman from the realty office, dropping the keys into Dan's palm like they were hot. "The Whipples couldn't take him. Florida. He's mostly an outside dog anyway."

Beth didn't like him. Hallie, who was nine, loved him immediately, the way kids do. Banjo ignored them all equally. He had one interest, and they found out what it was the third night, when the sound woke Dan at two in the morning: scrape, scrape, scrape, rising up through the floor registers like the house had an itch in its bones.

The cellar was fieldstone, a furnace like an iron octopus, a workbench with baby-food jars of screws nailed above it by their lids. The far end was dirt floor, where the ledge came up out of the ground like a whale's back. Banjo had dug a hole at the base of it the size of a bushel basket. His front paws were raw. The quicks of his nails had bled into the dirt, black as coffee grounds, and he looked up at Dan with an expression Dan would think about later — not guilt. Something like apology. The look of a creature doing what it had been made to do.

Dan filled the hole. Tamped it with the flat of the shovel. The dirt at the bottom had been warm. Not hot — warm, like asphalt at noon in July, and he stood there a minute with his hand in it, because it was October, in Maine, in a cellar.

Banjo dug it out again. Dan put a cinder block on the spot, a thirty-pounder he could barely carry one-handed, and in the morning the block was four feet away and the hole was deeper than the dog was tall, Banjo down in it up to his shoulders, working. He'd stopped eating by then. Wouldn't touch the kibble. Drank, though. Drank like a horse and went back down.

Earl Bonsaint, across the road, sat in a lawn chair in his dooryard from May to November and missed nothing. Dan carried him over a beer one evening. "Whipples move to Florida?" he asked.

"That's what they told you." Earl opened the beer with his pocketknife. "Well. Maybe they did. Real estate people'll tell you a lot." He drank. "They left stuff behind, I know that. Didn't come back for none of it."

There was stuff. Mason jars of green beans from 1987, furred with dust. A box of Reader's Digest Condensed Books. Under the workbench, a child's red rubber boot, small — a four-year-old's boot — gone gray. Hallie held it up and said, "Earl says the Whipples didn't have any kids," and Dan told her to put it down, that it was filthy, and later he went back and put it in the trash barrel himself, moving fast, not looking at it.

The smell started the second week. Sweet. Like apples gone soft in the grass. It came up through the registers at night along with the sound — scrape, scrape, pause, scrape — and Beth said, Portland has a vet school, Dan, there is something wrong with that animal, and Dan said yes, in the morning, and didn't sleep, because the hole had a breath now. He'd felt it on his face when he shone the flashlight down. In and out. Slow.

On the fifteenth night the sound changed. Got regular. Got a rhythm, like something keeping time, and Dan got out of bed and went down the hall and stopped, because Hallie was standing at the top of the cellar stairs in her nightgown, watching the door the way you'd watch a pot you weren't supposed to touch.

"He's almost through," she said.

Dan opened the cellar door. The light over the stairs had burned out and the smell came up at him, strong enough to taste, and the sound went on, patient, steady, from the dark at the far end where the ledge was. He stood there with his hand on the rail. Then Banjo came and stood beside him at the top of the stairs — Dan felt the fur brush his bare ankle — ears up, looking down into the dark, and down in the cellar the digging went on.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The Rail still smelled like fried onions and spilled beer, and the floorboards still creaked under the same sticky varnish. For a second, Wren let herself pretend the last twelve years were just a story she’d pitched and killed. Then the door opened.

She knew his hands before his face.

Grease worked into the creases of his knuckles. The scar across his thumb, pale and familiar. He hung his jacket on the same hook by the jukebox, shrugged out of the rain like he’d done it a thousand times, and when he turned, the whole room tilted.

Jonah Hale.

He saw her too. His shoulders stopped mid-shrug. Then he finished the motion, slow, deliberate, and walked to the bar. Not toward her. Not away. Right up to the stool two down from hers, like he was choosing the exact distance at which he could stand to hurt her.

“Bourbon,” he said to Mick. “Neat.”

Mick nodded, pretended not to feel the static. “Haven’t seen you in a while, Wren.”

“Just passing through.”

Jonah laughed, low and rough. “Ain’t that the truth.”

She should’ve left then. Her notebook was in the car. Her motel key. A dozen perfectly good exits.

Instead she turned. “Jonah.”

“Wren Caldwell.” He raised the glass without looking at her. “Back from the dead.”

“I’m not dead.”

“Could’ve fooled me.”

The words landed clean, no hesitation. Twelve years of practice, maybe. She deserved worse and she knew it.

“I read your bylines sometimes,” he said. “Big stories. Fancy paper. You always did want out.”

“I wanted a life.”

“You had one.” He finally looked at her, and whatever she’d expected—rage, longing, indifference—wasn’t there. It was worse. He looked tired. “You just didn’t stay long enough to notice.”

The rain hammered the windows. A truck passed on the highway, tires hissing.

“I’m here for work,” she said. “The plant closing. Profiles.”

“Convenient.”

“It’s not about you.”

“Nothing ever was.”

That stung. She wrapped both hands around her beer bottle, grounding herself in the cold glass. “I couldn’t say goodbye, Jonah. I tried. I sat on that porch with my bag packed and I couldn’t open the door.”

“You could’ve called.”

“I know.”

“You could’ve written.”

“I know.”

“You could’ve showed up at my old man’s funeral.”

Her throat tightened. “I didn’t know until six months after.”

“Yeah.” He knocked back the bourbon, set the glass down with a soft clink. “That’s the thing about leaving, Wren. You miss a lot.”

She wanted to touch him. The ridiculous, childish urge to reach across those two empty stools and press her palm to his jaw, to find out if he still leaned into her like he used to. She kept her hands where they were.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“Don’t.” He shook his head, pulled a few bills from his wallet. “Not tonight. Not when you’re just passing through.”

He stood. He was broader now, harder, the boy she’d loved layered under years of work and weather. For a moment neither of them moved.

Then Jonah leaned in, close enough that she caught the scent of motor oil and winter air, and said, “If you’re still here tomorrow, buy me breakfast. If you’re not, don’t bother with the apology next time either.”

He walked out. The door swung shut behind him, and the bell above it rang like a warning.

Wren sat alone in the smell of fried onions and old wood, staring at the empty stool, already knowing she wasn’t going anywhere.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
The fluorescent lights in Interview Room C hummed like an insect against glass. Mara Cline set her file down and slid into the chair across from Luis Morales, who sat with his hands folded around a paper cup of coffee he hadn’t touched.

“Thanks for coming in again,” she said.

Luis shrugged. He was forty-two, with the weathered look of a man who had spent two decades on loading docks. “Said I’d help. Jaylen’s a good kid.”

“He’s twenty-six, Luis. And he’s facing twenty years for armed robbery.”

“He didn’t do it.”

“That’s what you’ve told the police, the grand jury, and now me. Twice. You said Jaylen was at your apartment in the Bronx from nine o’clock until after midnight on March fourteenth.”

“That’s right.”

Mara opened the file and placed a printed photograph on the table. It showed the front of a bodega on Tremont Avenue, timestamped 9:17 p.m.

“The robbery happened at nine-fourteen,” she said. “Three blocks from your building. The clerk picked Jaylen out of a photo array. You’re the only person placing him anywhere else.”

“Because he was with me.”

“Doing what?”

“Watching the game. Knicks and Celtics.”

Mara slid another sheet across. “I pulled the cable guide. The Knicks played in Charlotte that night. The game started at seven, not nine. By nine-seventeen, it was halftime.”

Luis didn’t look at the paper. “Maybe it was the earlier game. I don’t remember exactly.”

“You were very specific in your statement.” Mara kept her voice level. “You said Jaylen complained about Randle missing free throws in the fourth quarter. That game wasn’t even close in the fourth. Randle didn’t go to the line after the third.”

A muscle tightened in Luis’s jaw. “So I got the night mixed up.”

“No, you didn’t.” Mara leaned forward. “You also said Jaylen helped you fix the hinge on your bathroom door. I went to your building yesterday. Your super let me look. The door is solid mahogany, hung with three-inch brass screws. The hinge wasn’t touched in months. There’s dust in the screw heads.”

Luis finally looked at her. “You got no right going through my apartment.”

“I had your consent. You signed the release.”

He pushed the coffee away. “Jaylen was there.”

“He wasn’t.” Mara pulled out a final photograph, this one a grainy still from a security camera in the lobby of Luis’s building. It showed the elevator bank at 9:09 p.m. A tall figure in a gray hoodie stood alone. “This is you, Luis. Where’s Jaylen?”

Luis stared at the image. His throat moved. “Maybe he took the stairs.”

“No entry on the stairwell camera either. Not at eight, not at nine, not at ten.” Mara let the silence hang. “You’re lying. And I need to know why, because in three days I have to put you on the stand, and the prosecutor is going to tear you apart.”

“He didn’t do it,” Luis said again, but his voice had thinned.

“I believe you think that. But an alibi only works if it’s true.” She tapped the photograph. “Who are you protecting?”

Luis’s eyes went to the door, as if someone might be listening. “I’m not protecting nobody.”

“There’s a difference between loyalty and sacrifice. Jaylen’s the one who’ll do the time. Not you. Not whoever actually walked into that bodega.”

“I don’t know who did the robbery.”

“But you know who Jaylen was with. Or where he really was.”

Luis pressed his palms flat against the table. “You don’t understand. Family is family.”

Mara felt the shift, the way the air in the room changed when a witness crossed from defiance to fear. “Whose family?”

Luis was quiet for a long moment. “My nephew, Mateo. He called me that night. Said he was in trouble. Needed me to say Jaylen was with me if anybody asked.”

“Why would Mateo need that?”

“Because Mateo was in that bodega. Not Jaylen.” Luis’s voice cracked. “He was the one with the gun. He was wearing Jaylen’s jacket. Same gray hoodie. Same build.”

Mara sat back, her pulse kicking. “You’re saying Mateo committed the robbery and let Jaylen take the fall.”

“I’m saying Jaylen lent him the jacket two days before. He didn’t know what Mateo was going to do.” Luis looked up, and for the first time his eyes were wet. “Mateo’s nineteen. He’s got a record. He’d go away forever. Jaylen’s clean. I thought… if I just held the line, maybe the cops wouldn’t have enough.”

“But they do,” Mara said quietly. “They have a mistaken eyewitness and your false alibi. Without the truth, Jaylen goes to prison for his cousin’s crime.”

Luis put his face in his hands. “What happens to Mateo if I tell you?”

“That’s not my call. But I can’t let an innocent man go to trial with a lie.” Mara reached across and touched his wrist. “You came here to help Jaylen. This is how you do it.”

Luis exhaled, shuddering. “I’ll tell you everything. But you have to promise you’ll keep Jaylen out of this.”

“I can’t promise that,” Mara said. “But I can promise I’ll finally be defending the right man.”

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The wind didn’t sound like wind anymore. It sounded like something alive and furious, throwing itself against the logs of the house because it knew we were inside. Warm. Alive. Two people who had run out of excuses to avoid each other.

I stared at the ceiling beam above the couch—*his* couch, leather cracked in the exact shape of a man who never sat still—and counted the fissures in the chinking. Forty-seven. I’d counted them twice yesterday and once before bed. It was easier than staring at Caleb Reid across the fire and pretending I didn’t notice the way his shoulders filled out a flannel shirt, or the way grief had carved him out in entirely different places than it had carved me.

Three days. We’d been snowed in for three days, two nights, and approximately thirty-six hours of conversational quicksand.

“You’re counting again.”

His voice came from the kitchen, rough as gravel over ice. I didn’t sit up. The blanket—the same one he’d wordlessly draped over me last night when I’d fallen asleep with a veterinary journal on my chest—smelled like cedar and him.

“I’m meditating,” I called back.

“You’re avoiding.” A cabinet slammed. “Coffee’s ready. If you want it, you’ll have to come get it. I’m not running room service.”

I closed my eyes. This was the game we played. He pushed; I retreated. I pushed; he retreated. We were both so good at it we could’ve earned medals, except the only prize was maintaining the brittle, careful distance between a man who thought needing anyone was a character flaw and a woman who had already buried the only person she’d ever sworn forever to.

*David.* His name came and went these days like a weather front—sometimes a hurricane, sometimes just a gray drizzle. This morning it was a whisper. I wasn’t sure if that was healing or betrayal.

I sat up, gathering the blanket around my shoulders like armor, and padded into the kitchen.

Caleb stood at the woodstove, back to me, pouring coffee into a mug that had seen better decades. He hadn’t shaved. The stubble darkened his jaw, tracing the sharp line down to where his collar hung open, revealing the top of a scar I’d caught a glimpse of yesterday when he’d hauled in another load of firewood. He moved like the ranch had taught him—economical, irritable, beautiful in the way untamed things are before they bite you.

“You sleep?” he asked, not turning around.

“Eventually.” I took the mug he extended without looking at me, our fingers brushing. I told myself the heat that shot up my arm was from the ceramic. “You?”

“Don’t sleep much.”

“Because you’re stubborn or because you’re busy brooding?”

That got me a glance, dark eyes flashing under brows that were currently drawn together in what I’d come to recognize as his default expression—suspicion mixed with something dangerously close to amusement.

“Because the generator makes a noise,” he said.

“It hums.”

“It whines.”

“You whine,” I muttered into my coffee.

He almost smiled. Almost. The left side of his mouth twitched, and I found myself staring at it like a starving woman offered bread. Three days of proximity had done terrible things to my defenses. I knew how he took his coffee—black, bitter, no sugar because sweetness was apparently a moral failing. I knew he checked the stock reports on a weathered radio every morning at six, jaw tight with worry for the cattle in the north pasture. I knew he had a photograph tucked in the drawer beneath the silverware of a woman with his eyes and a smile that didn’t reach them. His mother, maybe. Or someone else he’d failed to save.

I knew too much. And he knew me—knew that I talked to animals before I treated them, that I still wore my wedding ring on a chain beneath my sweater, that I cried in the bathroom yesterday for twelve minutes exactly because I’d found one of David’s old business cards in the depths of my wallet.

“Storm’s supposed to break tonight,” Caleb said, staring out the window at a wall of white.

“Supposed to.”

“Means you can get back to town. To your clinic. Your life.”

The way he said it—*your life*—made it sound like a verdict. Like he was already stacking the bricks between us, rebuilding the wall the blizzard had inconveniently knocked down.

“Means you get your solitude back,” I replied, keeping my voice light. “No more me cluttering up your couch, stealing your blankets, criticizing your coffee.”

He turned then, fully, leaning against the counter with his arms crossed. The stance should have been defensive. Instead, it framed the lean, hard lines of him in a way that made my mouth dry.

“You don’t clutter,” he said quietly.

My heart did something stupid and dangerous. *Don’t*, I told it. *We don’t do this. We don’t read meaning into the words of lonely men in snowstorms. We don’t replace ghosts with warm bodies.*

But the kitchen was small. The air between us felt charged, static before lightning.

“Caleb—”

“The hay in the barn roof is getting wet,” he interrupted, pushing off the counter, suddenly restless. “The wind shifted. I need to check the southeast corner. Make sure the tarp held.”

“You can’t go out there. The drifts are—”

“I know what they are, Elena.” My name in his mouth sounded like a confession. He grabbed his coat from the hook, movements sharp, angry. “I know my own land.”

“Knowing it and surviving it are two different things.”

He paused at the door, hand on the latch. For a second, the mask slipped, and I saw it—the fear, the wanting, the same raw edge I felt every time I looked at him and remembered what it was like to be known by someone.

“Yeah,” he said, his voice barely audible over the wind’s howl. “They are.”

Then he opened the door, and the storm swallowed him whole.

I stood there, clutching my coffee, listening to my own heart pound against my ribs. The ring on its chain suddenly felt heavy as an anchor.

Or maybe, for the first time in three years, it felt like a weight I was tired of carrying.

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The Buick smelled of old smoke and the pine air freshener that had been hanging off the mirror since before either of them owned it. Eddie sat angled against the passenger door with his hands pushed down between his knees, watching the duplex across the street. No lights yet. Ten to six by the dash clock, which ran nine minutes fast, which Ray knew and never fixed because he said a man ought to give himself nine extra minutes.

"He's not going anywhere," Ray said.

"That's not what I'm saying."

"Then say it again, only different."

Eddie rubbed his palms on his jeans. "Wheels was at the bar last night. You know what he told me? The Fuentes brothers. Remember them? They did a favor for Anton last winter, some collection thing, and they were supposed to get paid Friday." He turned his head. "Nobody's seen them since February. Wheels says the cousin got a card from Texas, but the cousin can't write."

"You believe everything you hear in a bar?"

"I believe the part where they're gone."

Ray took the cigar out of the ashtray and didn't light it, just rolled it between his fingers. He had a way of going still when he didn't like a conversation, like a dog hearing something under the porch.

"The job's a snatch, that's all," he said. "Sal skimmed from the laundries. Anton wants his money back and he wants Sal sitting somewhere quiet while the money finds its way home. We hold him at the cabin two, three days. Ten apiece. Nobody gets hurt."

"Then what's in the glovebox?"

"It's for convincing."

"And after we hand him over? Sal's seen my face. I've seen the face of the guy Anton sent to count the money. Loose ends, Ray. We're the loose ends. It ain't the Fuentes brothers' fault they disappeared, it's what they knew."

Across the street a school bus groaned past the corner, empty, its lights washing the frost off the parked cars. Ray watched it go.

"Kidnapping's federal," Eddie said. "You take a man in a car, they can make it federal. They got a whole floor of a building in Cleveland just for that."

"Who told you that, your sister?"

"My sister's a paralegal."

"Your sister answers phones."

"She answers phones at a law firm."

Ray put the cigar back in the tray. "I took five up front."

Eddie stared at him. The defroster had quit and the windows were fogging from their breath, the street going soft and gray outside the glass.

"You took half," Eddie said. "Before you even told me there was a job."

"I gave four of it to Womack. You want to be the one explains to Womack why I need it back?"

"You spent my half too?"

"I spent what there was."

Eddie laughed once, a short sound with nothing in it, and looked at the ceiling of the car. There was a tear in the headliner above the visor where someone had once pushed something up into it and thought better of it. "So I can't walk. You already walked for me. You cashed me."

"I got us a way out of the hole. You want to call it that instead?"

"What I want," Eddie said, "is to be twenty-six again and have somebody tell me don't."

The porch light came on across the street.

They both went quiet. The door of the duplex opened and Sal stepped out in a tan coat, the same man from the photograph, older-looking under the light, and behind him came a little girl in a purple backpack, maybe seven, her hair still flat on one side from sleep. Sal carried her down the two steps and opened the door of the Honda and leaned in to buckle her, his breath going white, and then he stood a moment with his hand on the top of the door like a man remembering something he'd forgotten.

Snow-delay morning, Eddie thought. Early drop-off. Somebody's life.

Ray's hand was on the key. Eddie could see the wedding ring he still wore, five years after the divorce, loose on him now. Ray had a girl in Elyria he hadn't seen since Easter. She'd be about twelve.

"Ray."

"I see her."

The hand stayed on the key. The little girl said something and Sal answered and closed her door gently, and the dome light went out, and the street was just a street again.

Ray turned the engine over and eased the Buick away from the curb without lights, then switched them on at the corner. Neither of them spoke past the gas station, past the on-ramp, the heater blowing cold.

"He'll send somebody else," Ray said finally. "You know that."

"Yeah."

"So it ain't on us."

Eddie didn't answer. In the side mirror, miles back now, he imagined the porch light still burning over the empty steps, patient as anything, waiting for whoever came next.

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
The dog started digging the second night, after the U-Haul was finally empty and the cardboard boxes had sweat through their bottoms in the hallway.

His name was Rufus, or Duke, or something the old owners had called him before they drove to Tucson to die near their daughter. Ben couldn’t remember and didn’t care. The animal had come with the house the way a bad odor comes with a used car—part of the paperwork, a handwritten note on yellow legal paper: *Please look after him. He is good with children.* Ben’s daughter, Alice, had fed him Spam from a plastic fork at lunch and the dog had licked her palm, and Ben had thought, *Fine. A week. Maybe two.*

Now it was nearly midnight and the scratching came from beneath the kitchen, rhythmic and patient, the sound of claws against packed earth.

Lydia stood at the cellar door in her oversized UConn sweatshirt, the one with the hole in the cuff. She held a mug of tea she wasn’t drinking. “He won’t come up.”

Ben listened. The house was old enough that the floorboards transmitted everything—mice, wind, the water heater’s asthmatic kick—but this was different. It had intention. “He’s a dog,” Ben said. “They dig.”

“He’s digging in the same spot.”

“I’ll go down in the morning.”

But in the morning the spot was a hole, and the hole was deeper than it should have been. Rufus—Duke?—sat beside it with dirt on his muzzle and a look Ben had never seen on a dog, a kind of embarrassed triumph, like a man caught with his hand in the offering plate. The cellar smelled of turned earth and something else, something sweet and corrupted, the smell of apples left to rot in a closed drawer.

Ben filled the hole with a shovel. The dirt was damp. He tamped it down with the flat of the blade and told the dog to go outside. The dog went up the stairs backwards, never taking his eyes off the filled hole.

That afternoon Alice found a bone.

Ben was at the sink trying to coax hot water from the faucet when she screamed. Not a real scream—a child’s theater scream, delighted and horrified at once. He took the stairs two at a time and found her kneeling in the dirt with something gray and curved in her hands. It was small, no bigger than a sparrow, and at first he thought it was a chicken bone. Then he saw the hinge. A jawbone, canine, with two long teeth still anchored in the rotted gum.

“Drop it,” Ben said, too loud.

Alice dropped it. The dog—Ben had decided the dog’s name was probably Rufus, after all—stood at the bottom of the stairs and whined, a thin sound like air escaping a tire.

Ben wrapped the bone in newspaper and threw it in the trash barrel outside. He scrubbed Alice’s hands with dish soap that smelled like fake lemons. He told Lydia it was a possum, maybe a raccoon. He did not tell her about the collar.

He had seen it when Alice turned the bone over in her hands: a strip of leather, green with mold, stamped with letters he couldn’t read. A dog’s collar, buried in the dirt beneath the house.

The second time, Ben went down with a flashlight.

It was past eleven. Lydia and Alice were asleep upstairs, the kind of sleep that follows exhaustion and cardboard pizza, and Ben sat at the kitchen table with a beer that had gone warm. The scratching had not stopped. It came in bursts, like Morse code. Scratch. Stop. Scratch scratch. Then a long pause, as if the dog were listening for an answer.

Ben opened the cellar door. The dog did not look up. He was at the far corner, where the foundation stones met the dirt floor, and he had dug a trench that ran the length of a man. The flashlight beam caught something pale in the wall. Not stone. Fabric.

Ben stepped closer. The smell was worse now, not apples but meat left in the sun, and beneath that a chemical sweetness he associated with hair salons and hospitals. Rufus wagged his tail once, a hesitant, apologetic wag, and kept digging.

The fabric was a shirt. Blue checked. It clung to something that had ribs.

Ben backed away. His heel caught the shovel and it clattered against the floor. The dog stopped. For a moment the cellar was silent except for the water heater’s tick. Then, from inside the wall, or from the dirt, or from somewhere too close to be anywhere else, something scratched back.

Rufus lowered his head and wagged his tail again, harder this time.
