Ben shut the cellar door. He did not lock it. He stood in the kitchen with the flashlight still on, the beam pointing at the ceiling, and he listened to the dog begin again.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The Situation Room had already emptied by the time Maya Ortiz reached the monitor. The President was gone, escorted upstairs by Secret Service, and only the stale coffee smell and the low hum of the ventilation remained. She’d been kept outside during the briefing—routine, they told her. Analysts did not present. Analysts wrote, stamped *SECRET/NOFORN*, and handed the truth upstairs.

But something had felt wrong from the moment she’d seen the courier leave her office. The folder had been thinner.

Maya slid her badge through the reader beside the secure terminal, pulled up the archived briefing packet, and scrolled to page seven. Her eyes locked on paragraph three.

*“…credible intelligence indicates an imminent kinetic threat from a DPRK submarine operating within fifty nautical miles of San Diego…”*

Her stomach turned. She had written the opposite.

She had written: *“No credible intelligence supports the presence of DPRK sub-surface assets off the U.S. West Coast. Single-source HUMINT remains unverified and is assessed as probable disinformation.”*

Someone had rewritten her assessment. And the President had just read the fake one.

Maya’s fingers flew across the keyboard, pulling the audit log. The timestamp told her everything. The file had been modified at 06:14 that morning, forty minutes before the briefing, from an account she didn’t recognize: *CVANCE_SCS3*.

“Colin,” she whispered.

She found Deputy Director Colin Vance in the corridor outside the Executive Secretariat, speaking in low tones with a man from the White House counsel’s office. Vance was fifty-two, silver-haired, with the kind of calm that made people trust him before he’d said anything worth trusting. He saw Maya coming and dismissed the lawyer with a touch on the elbow.

“Maya. I thought you’d gone home.”

“Who altered my briefing?”

Vance’s smile didn’t waver. “Walk with me.”

“I’m not walking anywhere. Page seven. That’s not my language. That’s not my assessment.”

He glanced up and down the empty corridor, then opened the door to a small SCIF-adjacent conference room. “Inside. Now.”

She stepped in. He closed the door.

“Sit,” he said.

“I’ll stand.”

“Suit yourself.” Vance settled into a chair and crossed his legs, as relaxed as if they were discussing quarterly budgets. “The briefing was adjusted for national security purposes.”

“Adjusted,” Maya repeated. “You fabricated an imminent North Korean attack.”

“We highlighted a contingency the President needed to consider.”

“A contingency? You changed a *negative* assessment into a *positive* threat. You inserted a location. A weapon system. A timeline. That’s not editing, Colin. That’s forgery.”

Vance steepled his fingers. “Your original report was incomplete. The HUMINT source—”

“Is a single walk-in who failed two polygraphs and couldn’t name the submarine’s hull number. I put that in the footnote. You removed the footnote.”

“The President doesn’t read footnotes, Maya. He reads conclusions.”

“Then he deserves the *right* conclusion.”

Vance’s tone cooled. “What the President deserves is clarity in a moment of strategic ambiguity. You want to talk about the truth? The truth is that Pyongyang has been probing our response patterns for eighteen months. The truth is that our Pacific assets are stretched thin. The truth is that a warning, even a precautionary one, moves resources into position before a threat becomes a catastrophe.”

“So you lie to him.”

“I correct the bias of an analyst who confuses caution with wisdom.”

Maya felt heat rise in her cheeks. “I’ve worked North Korean maritime intelligence for six years. I wrote the assessment because it’s what the data supports. If you wanted a different policy recommendation, you write your own memo. You sign your own name. You don’t put words in my mouth and send them to the Oval Office.”

Vance leaned forward. For the first time, the diplomat’s mask slipped. “You think this is about you? This is about a President who needs to authorize action before Congress, before the press, before our allies start asking why we look paralyzed. Sometimes the truth is a process, Maya. Not a product.”

“That’s not your call.”

“Actually, it is.” He stood, smoothing his tie. “I’m the Deputy Director of Operations Support. I supervise the dissemination of finished intelligence. I have the authority—”

“To alter raw analysis?”

“To contextualize it.”

She laughed, sharp and short. “You changed a probability judgment. You invented an imminent threat to the homeland. Do you know what happens when that leaks? Every word of that briefing came out of my directorate. My name is in the byline.”

“Your name is valuable. It gives the assessment credibility.”

“Credibility you exploited.”

Vance moved toward the door, then paused with his hand on the handle. “Let me explain how this ends if you push it. You file a complaint. Inspector General opens an inquiry. Six months later it concludes the changes fell within the Director’s discretionary authority. You get reassigned to the Kazakhstan desk, or worse, the records declassification team in Suitland. Your source access dries up. Your career becomes a footnote in a report nobody reads.”

He turned to face her. “Or you take a breath. You accept that there are levels to this work you haven’t reached yet. And tomorrow you write the follow-on assessment I ask you to write.”

Maya stared at him. “What follow-on?”

“The one that validates the President’s decision. Once he acts, the story needs to hold together.”

“You want me to clean up your lie.”

“I want you to be on the right side of history.”

Maya stepped closer. She was shorter than Vance by half a foot, but she didn’t blink. “Here’s what’s going to happen. I’m going to the IG tonight. I’m going to the staff director of the House Intelligence Committee. And I’m going to make sure the President knows that the paper he read this morning was not the paper I wrote.”

Vance studied her, his expression unreadable. Then he smiled again, smaller this time.

“You always were the brightest one in your cohort, Maya. I admired that about you.” He opened the door. “But brightness without judgment is just a fire looking for fuel. Be careful you don’t burn down everything you’re trying to protect.”

He walked out. The door clicked shut behind him.

Maya stood alone in the silent room. She reached into her pocket, pulled out her phone, and opened the encrypted voice recorder app she’d started the moment she entered. The red light blinked. She hit save.

Then she sat down, opened her laptop, and began to draft a memorandum—to the Inspector General, to the record, to whoever would listen.

She wrote the first sentence twice before she got it right.

*“The briefing delivered to the President at 07:00 hours on 14 October was not the briefing I prepared…”*

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The Crown Vic smelled like mildew and old cigarette smoke, a scent that seemed to rise from the bench seat whenever the humidity climbed above seventy. Vic kept the engine off. The streetlight three houses down flickered, buzzing like an insect against glass. He stared at the split-level with the slate-blue siding and the basketball hoop in the driveway, and his right hand drummed a slow, nervous rhythm against the steering wheel.

"I don't like it," Vic said.

Darnell shifted in the passenger seat, his knee bouncing against the cracked dash. "Man, you don't like the coffee, you don't like the weather. You don't like nothing."

"Upstairs light just came on. East-facing window."

"So? She’s awake. She goes to bed at eleven, like her sister said."

"That’s not her bedroom," Vic said. "That’s the kid’s room."

Darnell stopped bouncing. He leaned forward, squinting past the bug-spattered windshield. The amber glow from the upstairs window cut a pale rectangle across the lawn. "You can't know that."

"I watched the house for three days. She sleeps in the back, corner window. That one faces the front. And the silhouette is half the size."

Darnell pulled out his phone, thumbs flying. "Crystal said the boy was at his father's this week. Every week in July."

"Crystal's a junkie who sold her own television for forty dollars. Her word is worth about that much."

"She's the sister. She knows the schedule."

"She knows what she wants to know." Vic’s hand stopped drumming. He gripped the wheel at ten and two, the way an instructor might, deliberate and tight. "The kid is home, Darnell. That changes the arithmetic."

"Bullshit. We grab the woman when she takes out the trash. Two minutes. The kid sleeps through it, or he don't. He ain't the target."

Vic turned his head slowly. In the dark, his face looked like it had been carved from something harder than flesh—cheekbones sharp, eyes sunken from too little sleep. "I did five years in Green Haven for a bank job where nobody got so much as a paper cut. You know what they give you for kidnapping? Federal time. You know what they give you when a minor is involved?"

"I know what Theo gives you when you walk away from a seventy-thousand-dollar score. He gives you concrete shoes and a trip to the river."

"Theo's a mid-level hustler with a leased Lexus. Don't make him the bogeyman."

"He fronted me five grand, Vic. Five. I spent it. On my mother’s insulin, on the title loan, on keeping my lights on. I don't show up with that woman in the next forty-eight hours, Theo don't send a strongly worded letter. He sends cousins." Darnell’s voice cracked on the last word. He cleared his throat and stared out the side window. "I can't go back to looking over my shoulder. I done that my whole life. This is supposed to be the one that gets us clear."

Vic looked back at the house. A shadow moved behind the upstairs curtain—a small head, maybe eight years old, maybe ten, looking out at the street before the light snapped off. Vic felt something cold settle behind his sternum.

"You ever been inside?" Vic asked quietly.

"Inside what?"

"A cell. A real one, not the holding pen downtown. You ever had a door slam behind you and know it ain't opening for a decade?"

Darnell didn't answer.

"I have," Vic said. "And I swore the only way I'd go back is if I put myself there. Not because some twitchy kid talked me into a snatch job with half a playbook and a sister who smokes her own paycheck."

Darnell's jaw tightened. He reached into his jacket and for a moment Vic tensed, but the hand came out empty, just trembling slightly in the space between them. "I ain't twitchy. I'm desperate. There's a difference."

"Not from where I'm sitting."

The streetlight buzzed again and went dark, plunging the block into a blue-gray dusk. In the silence, Vic could hear Darnell’s breath, shallow and fast. He turned the key one click forward. The dash lit up, bathing them in pale green. Then he turned it back. The dark returned.

"Tomorrow," Vic said.

"What?"

"Kid leaves for his father's at nine in the morning. Crystal got that part right—I saw the duffel bag in the hall. We hit her when she gets back from the drop-off. No rush. No kids. Clean."

Darnell exhaled, a long shuddering release that fogged the lower corner of the windshield. He nodded, just once. "Tomorrow."

Vic settled back into the mildewed seat and watched the house. Neither of them spoke again. The cicadas screamed in the trees, loud enough to drown out second thoughts.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The first thing I smelled in Harrow was the graveyard, which was good news for my purse and bad for my appetite.

Moss smelled it too. He stopped in the middle of the road, nose up, ears tipped toward the hill above the village, and looked back at me. With Moss, that particular look is a question.

"Probably," I said. "But we get paid first. We're not doing noble before supper again."

He wagged once, which is his word for *agreed*, and trotted on ahead. Moss is an excellent dog. He never asks me to be a better person on an empty stomach.

We'd timed it right, coming in at dusk. Villages trust you more when you walk out of the dark instead of the daylight—I can't explain it, but I've learned to use it. The dark is where they think monsters come from, so when a girl with a sword comes out of it too, they figure she must be on their side. Also, the sun had been bright as a blade all afternoon and my head still rang with it, so dusk suited us fine. My father gave me almost nothing, as fathers go, but he did leave me eyes that see better at night and skin that burns by breakfast. Thanks, Da.

Three days out of Bellwether we'd spent the last of the tanner's silver, and the village before that had paid me in chickens. Moss is still not forgiven for the chickens.

Harrow was the usual: two dozen cottages, a chapel with a leaning bell, doors hung with hawthorn and garlic braids. The garlic doesn't do anything, by the way. It just makes the whole village smell like supper. I never tell them. Let people have their charms. Hope is cheaper than me.

A girl at the well froze when she saw us, bucket halfway up. I smiled with my mouth closed. I've learned to do that.

"Evening," I said. "Who do I talk to about the graves?"

She pointed, dripping, toward the biggest cottage, and ran.

The reeve was a man named Hobb, with a beard that had given up but a handshake that hadn't. He looked me over the way they all do—the sword first, then the teeth I wasn't showing, then Moss, who had parked himself on the man's boot as though it belonged to him now.

"You're the one off the notices?" he said. "The—ah—the slayer?"

"The notices say *discreet removal of the restless dead*," I said. "But yes."

"How much?"

"Five silver for a ghoul. Eight for a wight. A revenant's twelve—they remember being people, and they fight like it. If it talks, that's extra."

"Extra for talking."

"Words cost me something," I said. "Seems fair they cost you something too."

He did the arithmetic that poor men do fast, and I watched him decide not to offer me chickens. "Supper and a bed in the bargain," he said, "and it's ten."

"How many?" I asked.

"One."

I waited. Villages don't send for me over one.

"One what?"

"Revenant." He said it like a curse. "The miller's boy, Wat. Drowned in the spring flood. Come back three nights running."

"Any attacks?"

"No." His voice went strange, then. "That's the thing of it. He doesn't *do* anything. He stands at the edge of the barley, facing the village, till cockcrow. Last night old Tam the shepherd got drunk enough to be brave and walked out to him. Says the boy spoke. Civil as you like."

I felt it then, the way you feel weather coming—a pressure behind the ears, a taste like a coin on the tongue. Some of that's the blood in me. Some of it's just seven years of this work.

"What did he say?"

Hobb studied his boots. Moss had gone very still beside me, which he only does when he thinks I should be paying attention. Traitor.

"He asked if the half-blood had come to the village yet," Hobb said. "Knew the name off the notices, miss. He asked for Vesper."

The wind came down off the hill, smelling of cold earth and opened graves, and under it—faint, familiar, wrong—something that smelled almost like me.

"Well, Moss," I said. "That's new."

Moss's considered opinion was that we should have been paid in advance.
